questions.stem: A Lambda function must query an Amazon RDS database in private subnets of a VPC. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Put the function in the private subnets, with a security group the database allows
options.rationale: The function then gets network interfaces in the VPC and can reach the database.

options.text: Add a NAT gateway to the VPC so that the function can reach the database through it
options.rationale: A NAT gateway is for outbound internet access; the database is already inside the VPC.

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the private subnets
options.rationale: Internet gateways do not help traffic that stays inside the VPC.

options.text: Give the execution role permission to create and manage network interfaces
options.rationale: Lambda needs these permissions, such as those in the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policy, to create its VPC interfaces.

options.text: Make the database publicly accessible
options.rationale: Exposing the database is unnecessary and weakens security.

questions.explanation: VPC access needs subnets, security groups and an execution role that can manage network interfaces.

questions.stem: A Lambda function connected to private subnets in a VPC must also call a public third-party API, and the calls time out. The VPC already has a public subnet with a route to an internet gateway. Which combination of steps will fix this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the function to the public subnet so that it can use the internet gateway
options.rationale: Connecting a function to a public subnet does not give it internet access, because its network interfaces have no public IP.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in the public subnet
options.rationale: The NAT gateway gives resources in private subnets outbound internet access through the public subnet.

options.text: Increase the function's timeout so the calls have more time
options.rationale: More time does not create a network path to the internet.

options.text: Route 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway in the private subnets' route table
options.rationale: The route sends the function's internet-bound traffic through the NAT gateway.

options.text: Add a route from the private subnets to the internet gateway
options.rationale: Without public IPs, the function cannot use an internet gateway directly; private subnets reach the internet through NAT.

questions.explanation: A VPC-connected function has no public IP, so internet access needs a NAT gateway in a public subnet plus a route to it from the private subnets. Moving the function to a public subnet is the trap: that alone does not give it internet access.

questions.stem: The same Lambda function code is deployed to development and production. Each environment uses a different DynamoDB table name. How should the function get the table name?

options.text: Hardcode both names and choose one with an if statement
options.rationale: Hardcoding ties configuration to code and needs a code change for new environments.

options.text: Read it from an environment variable set for each environment
options.rationale: Environment variables change configuration without changing code.

options.text: Create a separate layer for each environment that contains the name
options.rationale: Layers package shared code and libraries; they are a clumsy way to hold settings.

options.text: Pass the name in the handler setting
options.rationale: The handler setting names the function's entry point, not configuration values.

questions.explanation: Environment variables keep environment-specific settings out of the deployment package.

questions.stem: A Lambda function that processes uploaded files fails with the message "Task timed out" on larger files. What should the developer change first?

options.text: Increase the function's reserved concurrency
options.rationale: Concurrency controls how many copies run at once, not how long each may run.

options.text: Turn on provisioned concurrency
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts; it does not extend the time limit.

options.text: Increase the function's timeout setting
options.rationale: The function is stopped when it reaches its configured timeout, so larger files need more time.

options.text: Add a layer with the file-processing library
options.rationale: Moving code into a layer does not change how long the function may run.

questions.explanation: "Task timed out" means the function reached its configured timeout, so raise the timeout to cover the longest run. Concurrency settings are the trap: they control how many copies run, not how long each may run.

questions.stem: A CPU-intensive Lambda function takes too long to finish. Which change is most likely to make it run faster?

options.text: Increase the function's timeout
options.rationale: A longer timeout lets the function run longer but does not make it faster.

options.text: Increase the function's ephemeral storage
options.rationale: More /tmp space helps with large files, not CPU-bound work.

options.text: Set reserved concurrency on the function
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency limits or guarantees instances; it does not speed up one invocation.

options.text: Increase the function's memory setting
options.rationale: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, so more memory also means more CPU.

questions.explanation: "CPU-intensive" is the clue: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, so more memory makes the function faster. A longer timeout is the trap; it lets a slow run finish but does not speed it up.

questions.stem: A Lambda function is invoked asynchronously. Events that still fail after Lambda's retries must be kept in an Amazon SQS queue for later reprocessing. Which configurations will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A dead-letter queue on the function that points to the queue
options.rationale: A function DLQ receives asynchronous events that fail all retry attempts.

options.text: An event source mapping on the function that reads from the queue
options.rationale: An event source mapping makes the function consume the queue, not write failures to it.

options.text: An on-failure destination that points to the queue
options.rationale: Destinations send failed asynchronous events, with details about the failure, to the target.

options.text: An on-success destination that points to the queue
options.rationale: On-success destinations receive successful invocations, not failures.

options.text: Reserved concurrency set to zero
options.rationale: Zero reserved concurrency throttles every invocation.

questions.explanation: For asynchronous invocations, use an on-failure destination (more detail) or a dead-letter queue to keep failed events.

questions.stem: A Lambda function processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue in batches. When one message in a batch fails, the whole batch is retried, and messages that succeeded are processed again. How can the developer retry only the failed messages?

options.text: Turn on partial batch responses and return the IDs of the failed messages
options.rationale: With ReportBatchItemFailures, only the listed messages return to the queue.

options.text: Increase the queue's visibility timeout so failed batches are retried later
options.rationale: A longer visibility timeout delays retries but still retries the whole batch.

options.text: Switch to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue
options.rationale: FIFO adds ordering; it does not change how a failed batch is retried.

options.text: Increase the function's memory
options.rationale: More memory does not change which messages are retried.

questions.explanation: Partial batch responses stop successful messages from being processed again.

questions.stem: Twenty Lambda functions use the same data-access library. The team wants to package the library once instead of including it in every function's deployment package. What should the developer use?

options.text: A Lambda extension
options.rationale: Extensions run alongside the function for tasks such as monitoring; they are not for sharing libraries.

options.text: A Lambda layer that contains the library
options.rationale: Functions reference the layer, so the code is packaged once; a new library version becomes a new layer version that each function then references.

options.text: An environment variable that holds the library code
options.rationale: Environment variables hold small settings, not code.

options.text: A larger ephemeral storage setting
options.rationale: Storage size has nothing to do with sharing code between functions.

questions.explanation: Layers share libraries, custom runtimes and other dependencies across functions.

questions.stem: During traffic spikes, a Lambda function opens so many database connections that the database rejects new ones. The developer wants to cap how many copies of the function can run at the same time. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Provisioned concurrency for the function
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm; it does not cap concurrency.

options.text: A longer timeout for the function
options.rationale: Longer runs would hold connections longer and make the problem worse.

options.text: Reserved concurrency for the function
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency sets the maximum number of concurrent instances of the function.

options.text: More memory for the function
options.rationale: Memory changes speed, not how many instances run.

questions.explanation: The clue is capping how many copies run at once, which is what reserved concurrency does. Provisioned concurrency is the nearest distractor, but it keeps instances warm and does not cap concurrency.

questions.stem: A Lambda function must process every item that is added or changed in a DynamoDB table, shortly after the change. What should the developer set up?

options.text: Create an Amazon S3 event notification for the table
options.rationale: S3 event notifications apply to S3 buckets, not DynamoDB tables.

options.text: Schedule a function to scan the whole table every minute and compare it with the last scan
options.rationale: Repeated scans are costly and can miss or duplicate changes.

options.text: Send AWS CloudTrail data events for the table to the function
options.rationale: CloudTrail records API activity for auditing; it is not a change-processing feed.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table and create an event source mapping for the function
options.rationale: Lambda polls the stream and invokes the function with batches of change records.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams plus an event source mapping is the standard way to react to item changes.

questions.stem: A Lambda function processes records from an Amazon Kinesis data stream. One malformed record makes the function fail, and the shard stops making progress while Lambda retries the same batch. Which combination of event source mapping settings will fix this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn on splitting the batch when the function returns an error
options.rationale: Bisecting the batch isolates the bad record so the good records can be processed.

options.text: Increase the batch size
options.rationale: A bigger batch still contains the bad record and still fails.

options.text: Increase the parallelization factor
options.rationale: More concurrent batches per shard do not get past a record that always fails.

options.text: Limit the retry attempts and send failed records to an on-failure destination
options.rationale: After the limit, Lambda records the failure and moves on instead of blocking the shard.

options.text: Add a dead-letter queue to the function's asynchronous invocation settings
options.rationale: Stream event source mappings do not use the function's asynchronous DLQ; they use their own on-failure destination.

questions.explanation: For stream sources, bisect on error, a retry limit or maximum record age, and an on-failure destination keep a poison record from blocking the shard.

questions.stem: A company wants every Lambda function to send its logs to a third-party monitoring service. The team does not want to change any function code. What should the developer add to the functions?

options.text: A Lambda extension, added as a layer, that uses the Telemetry API
options.rationale: Extensions run alongside the function and can receive its logs and telemetry without code changes.

options.text: A logging library in each function that sends log lines over HTTPS
options.rationale: That requires a code change in every function.

options.text: A larger memory setting so that logs are flushed to the service faster
options.rationale: Memory does not route logs anywhere.

options.text: An environment variable that holds the monitoring service's URL
options.rationale: A variable alone does nothing unless code or an extension reads it.

questions.explanation: Lambda extensions, delivered as layers, integrate monitoring and security tools without changing function code.

questions.stem: A Lambda function downloads a 3 GB file to /tmp to process it, and fails with a "No space left on device" error. What should the developer change?

options.text: Increase the function's memory setting
options.rationale: Memory and /tmp storage are configured separately.

options.text: Increase the function's ephemeral storage
options.rationale: The /tmp size is configurable, so the file fits.

options.text: Increase the function's timeout
options.rationale: The error is about disk space, not time.

options.text: Add a Lambda layer that contains the large file
options.rationale: Layers are read-only, deployment-time content and count against a deployment size limit; they are not scratch space.

questions.explanation: Ephemeral storage (/tmp) has its own setting, separate from memory.

questions.stem: A developer renamed a Node.js Lambda function's file from index.js to app.js and redeployed. Every invocation now fails with Runtime.HandlerNotFound. What should the developer change?

options.text: The function's runtime to a newer Node.js version
options.rationale: The runtime is fine; Lambda cannot find the handler at the configured location.

options.text: The execution role, to allow lambda:InvokeFunction
options.rationale: The error is about locating code, not permissions.

options.text: The function's handler setting, to app.handler
options.rationale: The handler setting names the file and exported function that Lambda calls.

options.text: The function's memory setting
options.rationale: Memory does not affect where Lambda looks for the handler.

questions.explanation: The handler setting must match the file name and exported function name.

questions.stem: A Lambda function is invoked asynchronously. After each successful invocation, its result must be sent to an Amazon EventBridge event bus, without adding code to the function. What should the developer configure?

options.text: A dead-letter queue that points to the event bus
options.rationale: A DLQ receives only failed events, and only SQS queues or SNS topics.

options.text: Reserved concurrency of 1
options.rationale: Concurrency does not route results.

options.text: An event source mapping from the event bus
options.rationale: That would make the bus a source of invocations, not a target for results.

options.text: An on-success destination for the event bus
options.rationale: Destinations send the invocation record, including the result, to the target after success or failure.

questions.explanation: For asynchronous invocations, destinations route success and failure records to SQS, SNS, Lambda or EventBridge.

questions.stem: A Lambda function processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue and writes to a third-party API that allows only a few calls at a time. The same function is also invoked directly by other callers, which must not be limited. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Maximum concurrency on the SQS event source mapping
options.rationale: This caps how many concurrent invocations the queue can drive, without limiting other callers.

options.text: Reserved concurrency on the function, set to a low value
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency caps every caller of the function, including the direct callers.

options.text: A longer visibility timeout on the queue
options.rationale: That changes when failed messages reappear, not how many run at once.

options.text: A delivery delay on the queue
options.rationale: Delaying messages does not cap how many are processed at the same time.

questions.explanation: Maximum concurrency on an SQS event source limits that source alone; reserved concurrency limits the whole function.

questions.stem: An application uses the AWS SDK to invoke a Lambda function that sends a welcome email. The application does not need the result and should not wait for the email to be sent. How should it invoke the function?

options.text: With the invocation type set to RequestResponse
options.rationale: This is a synchronous call that waits for the function to finish.

options.text: With the invocation type set to Event
options.rationale: Lambda queues the event and returns immediately; the function runs asynchronously.

options.text: With the invocation type set to DryRun
options.rationale: DryRun only checks that the caller is allowed to invoke the function; the function does not run.

options.text: Through a Lambda function URL
options.rationale: A function URL invokes the function synchronously.

questions.explanation: InvocationType Event makes an asynchronous invocation; RequestResponse waits for the result.

questions.stem: A Lambda function is triggered when images are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. It writes a resized copy of each image back to the same bucket, and the number of invocations keeps growing. Which changes will stop this loop? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase the function's reserved concurrency
options.rationale: More concurrency lets the loop grow faster.

options.text: Increase the function's timeout
options.rationale: The loop comes from new events, not from slow invocations.

options.text: Limit the trigger to an uploads/ prefix and write resized images under another prefix
options.rationale: The function's own writes no longer match the event notification's filter.

options.text: Add a dead-letter queue to the function
options.rationale: The invocations do not fail, so nothing goes to the DLQ.

options.text: Write the resized images to a different bucket
options.rationale: Writes no longer land where the trigger listens.

questions.explanation: A function that writes to the location that triggers it creates a recursive loop. Use a separate bucket or non-overlapping prefixes.

questions.stem: A Lambda function reads a DynamoDB stream but must act only on newly inserted items. It currently runs for every insert, update and delete, and returns early for most of them. How can the developer stop the unneeded invocations?

options.text: Change the stream's view type from NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES to KEYS_ONLY
options.rationale: The view type changes what each record contains, not which records invoke the function.

options.text: An if statement at the start of the handler
options.rationale: The function would still be invoked, and billed, for every record.

options.text: A filter on the event source mapping that matches INSERT events
options.rationale: Event filtering drops records that do not match before the function is invoked.

options.text: A batch size of 1 on the event source mapping
options.rationale: Smaller batches mean more invocations, not fewer.

questions.explanation: Event source mappings can filter records, so the function is invoked only for records that match.

questions.stem: A Lambda function is invoked asynchronously to send time-sensitive alerts. When the function is throttled, Lambda keeps retrying events for hours, and stale alerts go out late. Events older than 10 minutes should be discarded. What should the developer configure?

options.text: The function's timeout, set to 10 minutes so that old events expire
options.rationale: The timeout limits how long one invocation runs, not how long an event waits in the queue.

options.text: Reserved concurrency of 0
options.rationale: That throttles every invocation.

options.text: A visibility timeout of 10 minutes
options.rationale: Visibility timeout is an Amazon SQS setting, not part of asynchronous invocation.

options.text: The maximum event age in the asynchronous invocation settings
options.rationale: Lambda discards events that wait longer than this age, or sends them to a configured destination.

questions.explanation: Asynchronous invocation settings include the retry attempts and the maximum age of an event.

questions.stem: A payment-processing Lambda function is sometimes throttled when other functions in the same account and Region use up the available concurrency. The payment function must always be able to scale to 100 concurrent executions. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Reserved concurrency of 100 on the payment function
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency sets aside that much of the account's concurrency for the function, so other functions cannot use it.

options.text: Provisioned concurrency of 100 on the other functions
options.rationale: This makes the other functions use more of the pool, not less.

options.text: A longer timeout on the payment function
options.rationale: The timeout limits how long one invocation runs; it does not set aside capacity.

options.text: A dead-letter queue on the payment function
options.rationale: A DLQ keeps failed asynchronous events; it does not prevent throttling.

questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency both guarantees and caps a function's share of the account's concurrency.

questions.stem: A team packages a Lambda function as a container image built from its own base image instead of an AWS base image. The image builds and pushes, but invocations fail because Lambda cannot talk to the function. What must the image include?

options.text: An EXPOSE instruction for port 8080 in the Dockerfile
options.rationale: Lambda does not reach functions through an exposed port.

options.text: The Lambda runtime interface client
options.rationale: Images not built on an AWS base image must add the runtime interface client so Lambda can pass events to the code.

options.text: The AWS CLI, installed in the image's final layer
options.rationale: The CLI is not how Lambda delivers events to the code.

options.text: A HEALTHCHECK instruction that calls the handler
options.rationale: Lambda does not use Docker health checks to invoke functions.

questions.explanation: Custom images need the runtime interface client; AWS base images already include it.

questions.stem: An API Gateway REST API has the resource /orders/{orderId} with a Lambda proxy integration. Where does the function find the value of orderId in the event?

options.text: In event.queryStringParameters.orderId
options.rationale: That map holds query string values, such as ?orderId=1, not path segments.

options.text: In event.body, parsed as JSON
options.rationale: The body holds the request payload, not the path.

options.text: In event.pathParameters.orderId
options.rationale: Proxy integrations pass path parameters to the function in the pathParameters map.

options.text: In the function's environment variables
options.rationale: Environment variables are set per function, not per request.

questions.explanation: The proxy event includes the path, path parameters, query string parameters, headers and body.

questions.stem: A developer adds a Lambda event source mapping to an existing DynamoDB stream. The function must also process the records that are already in the stream, not only new ones. Which starting position should the developer choose?

options.text: LATEST
options.rationale: LATEST starts with records written after the mapping is created, so existing records are skipped.

options.text: AT_TIMESTAMP set to the current time
options.rationale: AT_TIMESTAMP is not supported for DynamoDB Streams event sources; it applies to sources such as Kinesis.

options.text: A batch size of 1
options.rationale: Batch size controls how many records each invocation gets, not where reading starts.

options.text: TRIM_HORIZON
options.rationale: TRIM_HORIZON starts from the oldest record still available in the stream.

questions.explanation: For stream sources, TRIM_HORIZON reads from the oldest available record and LATEST from new records.

questions.stem: A Lambda function appends each request's items to a list that is declared outside the handler. Users sometimes see items from other users' requests in their responses. What is the cause?

options.text: Reused execution environments keep the list between invocations
options.rationale: Code outside the handler runs once per environment, and its variables persist across the invocations it serves.

options.text: Lambda runs several requests in the same invocation at once
options.rationale: Each invocation handles one event; the leak comes from reused global state.

options.text: The function's memory setting is too low for the list
options.rationale: Low memory causes errors, not data from other requests.

options.text: The list is written to the shared /tmp folder of the Region
options.rationale: Variables live in memory, and /tmp belongs to one execution environment.

questions.explanation: Initialize per-request data inside the handler. Reuse globals only for things such as SDK clients and connections.

questions.stem: Other services in the company's AWS accounts need to call a single Lambda function over HTTPS. The team wants the simplest setup, and callers will sign requests with their IAM credentials. What should the developer configure?

options.text: A function URL with the NONE auth type
options.rationale: NONE lets anyone with the URL call the function without signing.

options.text: A function URL with the AWS_IAM auth type
options.rationale: A function URL gives the function its own HTTPS endpoint, and AWS_IAM requires SigV4-signed requests.

options.text: An Application Load Balancer with the function as a target
options.rationale: An ALB authenticates users through OIDC or Amazon Cognito, not IAM-signed requests, and it adds a load balancer the simplest setup does not need.

options.text: An Amazon SQS queue that the function polls for requests
options.rationale: A queue is asynchronous, not an HTTPS request and response.

questions.explanation: Function URLs are a simple HTTPS endpoint for one function. AWS_IAM auth requires signed requests, and callers in other accounts also need permission in the function's resource-based policy.
